1.3 Components of HCI
Human-Computer Interaction relies on several primary components that work
together.
i) User (صارف)
Any individual or group that interacts with a computer system to achieve defined
goals. Classified into two categories:

ii) Computer System (سسٹم کمپیوٹر)
The platform where humans and computers communicate through input, output, and
feedback using an interface. It connects human actions with machine responses.
iii) User Interaction (تعامل کا صارف)
The process through which a user communicates with a system by performing
actions (clicking, tapping, typing, speaking). It transforms user intent into system
responses. (Types detailed on next page).
iv) Task (کام)
The specific action users perform (e.g., booking a ticket). Characteristics include:
Task Complexity: Difficulty level (filling a form vs designing a 3D model).
User Knowledge: Skills required (basic typing vs advanced programming).
Time Requirement: Duration needed (ATM withdrawal vs online passport application).

v) User Interface (UI)
The medium through which humans interact with computer systems.
Graphical User Interface (GUI): Uses visual elements like windows, icons, and menus (e.g.,
Windows OS, Android).
Command-Line Interface (CLI): Uses text-based typing (e.g., MS-DOS, Linux Terminal).
Touch Interface: Interaction via gestures like tapping, swiping, pinching (e.g., Smartphones,
Tablets).
Voice User Interface (VUI): Interacting through spoken commands (e.g., Smart Speakers).
Natural User Interface (NUI): Relies on gestures, body movements, or immersive
environments (e.g., VR Headsets, Microsoft Kinect).
vi) Environment
The real-world setting where a person uses a computer system. It is shaped by physical
conditions (e.g., an ATM outdoors in sunlight), social conditions (e.g., a quiet classroom),
and technical hardware.
vii) Feedback
The signal or response given to confirm or guide actions.
System Feedback
Response from the computer (e.g., "Loading..."
bar, "Message Sent!" tick mark, or an Error
sound).
User Feedback
Input from the user to the system (e.g.,
tapping a "Submit" button, giving a 5-star
rating).

1. High Contrast (رنگ واضح)
Making text and pictures stand out clearly against the background. Example: Black text on

large "Calibri" font makes homework instructions easy to read.

sections.heading: 1.7 Human Computer Interaction Problems
sections.body:
1.7 Human Computer Interaction Problems
★ GOLDEN TOPIC
HCI problems are common difficulties that stop users from using technology
smoothly. These happen when systems fail to meet human needs or cognitive
limits.
Problem
Explanation & Example
Interface
Complexity
Too many options or a confusing layout.
Example: A shopping app with so many menus you can't find the
checkout button.
Poor Feedback
The system doesn't show if an action worked or failed.
Example: Clicking "Submit" on a form and the screen just freezes
without a confirmation message.
Inconsistency
Different parts of the app look or act differently.
Example: Using a magnifying glass icon for "Search" on one
page, but a binocular icon on another.
Accessibility Gaps
Design ignores people with disabilities.
Example: A video tutorial platform without text captions for deaf
users.
Compatibility
Issues
Interface fails on different devices or browsers.
Example: A website that works perfectly on a laptop but crashes
on a mobile browser.

sections.heading: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI
sections.body:
1.8 Methods for Improving HCI
Enhance Usability: Simplify navigation. (e.g., A clear "Buy Now" button).
Strengthen Accessibility: Support disabilities. (e.g., Captions on videos).
Ensure Consistency: Keep layouts uniform. (e.g., Same "Save" button everywhere).
Provide Clear Feedback: Show action results. (e.g., "Payment Successful" popup).
Improve Adaptability: Responsive design. (e.g., Website scales to mobile screens).
Apply User-Centered Design (UCD): Focus on real user goals and pilot test.
Use Multimodal Interaction: Allow touch, voice, or gesture inputs combined.
Continuous Testing: Regularly update based on user feedback.

sections.heading: 1.9.2 User Experience (UX)

1.9.2 User Experience (UX)
UX refers to the overall experience a user has while interacting with a system—
how smooth, comfortable, and satisfying it feels.
UI is what you see; UX is how it feels.
Example: In a Food Delivery App, the UI is the nice pictures of burgers and red buttons. The UX is
the fact that the app loads fast, tracking works perfectly, and the food arrives without the user
getting frustrated.

Career Opportunities in UI/UX
UX Designer: Researches user needs to ensure the app is intuitive and satisfying.
UI Designer: Designs the visual layout (colors, typography, buttons) using tools like Figma.
Interaction Designer: Focuses on the flow between screens, animations, and gestures.
Usability Researcher: Runs SUS/NPS tests and A/B tests with real users to find flaws.
Accessibility Specialist: Ensures products meet inclusive standards for people with
disabilities.
Summary
HCI: The study of how people and computers interact to create human-centered
technology.
Interaction Modes: Sight, Touch, Hearing, Voice, Spatial.

2.3.1 Number of Steps (Big O Notation)
When discussing efficiency, we focus on how an algorithm's performance is
affected as the input size (n) increases. Big O Notation is a mathematical
method used to describe how the running time or memory usage grows as the
input size increases.

sections.heading: 1. Constant Time - O(1)
sections.body:
1. Constant Time - O(1)
The execution time remains constant regardless of the input size. Whether the dataset has
10 elements or 10 million, the operation takes the same time.
Example: Accessing the first element of an array (arr[0]).

sections.heading: 2. Linear Time - O(n)
sections.body:
2. Linear Time - O(n)
The execution time increases proportionally with the input size. If the input doubles, the
time doubles.
Example: Linear search in an unsorted list (checking every item one by one).
Big O Notation (Continued)

sections.body:
3. Logarithmic Time - O(log n)
The execution time increases very slowly as the input grows. The algorithm repeatedly
reduces the problem size by half, making it highly efficient for massive datasets.
Example: Binary search on a sorted list.

sections.body:

The execution time increases proportionally to the square of the input size. Commonly
occurs with nested loops. Highly inefficient for large datasets.
Example: Bubble Sort or comparing every item in a list against every other item.

2.4 Refinements to improve clarity
Improving an algorithm involves reviewing it step by step—simplifying logic,
removing redundant work, and picking smart data structures. A clear algorithm
is easier to follow.

i) Use Meaningful Names
Replace vague variables with descriptive ones.
Bad: a = b / c
Good: average = totalSum / totalItems
ii) Break into Modules
Instead of a massive block of logic, divide the process into separate, manageable
functions. (e.g., separating the CalculateSum() function from the main printing logic).
iii) Improve Structure & Indentation
Proper visual formatting reduces the mental effort needed to read the code. Deeply
packed loops and IF statements become confusing without proper spacing.
iv) Add Comments
Keep comments short and meaningful. Explain why something is done, not just what is
happening, especially for tricky logic sections.

sections.heading: 2.4.2 Refinements to improve Efficiency
sections.body:
2.4.2 Refinements to improve Efficiency
i) Reduce Unnecessary Steps
Eliminate redundant operations. For example, in Bubble Sort, after the first pass, the largest
value settles at the end. The algorithm should be optimized to ignore that sorted portion in
the next pass, shrinking the inner loop and saving operations.
ii) Use Better Algorithms
Pick the algorithm that fits the situation. If you need to search a list of 1 million sorted
records, replacing Linear Search with Binary Search changes execution time from seconds
to milliseconds.
iii) Avoid Re-computing Values
If a calculation results in a fixed value that won't change, do not calculate it inside a loop.
Compute it once, store it in a variable, and reuse it (Memoization/Caching).
# BAD: Re-computing C repeatedly

C = A + B
Print C * i
End For
# GOOD: Compute C once outside
C = A + B
For i = 1 to N
Print C * i
End For
iv) Use Appropriate Data Structures
Choosing the right data structure (Array, Linked List, Tree) is like picking the right tool for a
job. If you need direct access, use an Array. If data is hierarchical, use a Tree. Do not force
one structure everywhere.

Dictionaries are highly dynamic. You can add new keys or change existing

d = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
# Modifying an existing value

# Adding a NEW Key-Value pair

# Deleting a Key-Value pair using 'del'

The Duplicate Keys Rule
A dictionary cannot have two identical keys. If you try to define a key more than
once, Python will not crash. Instead, the last assigned value wins, silently
overwriting previous values.

print(d)

3.1.7 Activity: Word Frequency Counter
Scenario: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence. This
demonstrates the power of Dictionaries and the .get() method.
# Sentence to analyze
sentence = "python is easy python is fun python is powerful"
# Split sentence into a list of words based on spaces
words = sentence.split()
# Empty dictionary for counting
word_freq = {}
# Count each word
for word in words:
# .get(word, 0) returns 0 if word is new, else returns its current count.
# Then we add 1.
word_freq[word] = word_freq.get(word, 0) + 1
print(f"Sentence: '{sentence}'\n")
print("Word Frequency Table:")
# Print formatted table
for word, count in word_freq.items():
print(f"{word:<10} : {count}")
# Find Most repeated word using max()
top_word = max(word_freq, key=word_freq.get)
print(f"\nMost Frequent: '{top_word}' ({word_freq[top_word]} times)")
🧠 Code Logic Breakdown
1. sentence.split() turns the string into ['python', 'is', 'easy', ...].
2. word_freq.get(word, 0) + 1 is the heart of the counter. It safely handles both brand
new words (starts at 0+1) and existing words (adds 1 to current count).
3. {word:<10} in the f-string forces the word to take up 10 spaces, perfectly aligning the
colons in the output table.

data = {
"Name": ["Ali", "Sara", "Ahmed", "Ayesha"],
"Marks": [85.0, None, 78.0, 92.0],  # Sara has missing marks
"Grade": ["A", "A", None, "A"]        # Ahmed has missing grade
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
Step 1: Check for Missing Values
Use isnull() to identify them. It returns True if a value is missing.
print(df.isnull())
Step 2: Count Missing Values
Use isnull().sum() to count exactly how many missing values exist in each column.
print(df.isnull().sum())
# Output will show Marks: 1, Grade: 1
Handling Missing Values (Continued)
Once missing values are found, you have two choices: replace them (fill) or
delete them (drop).
Step 3: Replace Missing Values (Fill)
Use fillna(). A common statistical trick is to replace a missing numeric value with the
average (mean) of that column.
# Replace missing Marks with the average of the Marks column
avg_marks = df["Marks"].mean()
df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(avg_marks)
# Replace missing Grade with a custom text
df["Grade"] = df["Grade"].fillna("Not Assigned")
print(df)
Alternative Step: Remove Rows (Drop)
If replacing data is not safe, you can completely delete any row that contains a NaN value
using dropna().
# Removes ANY row that has at least one missing value
df = df.dropna()
print(df)

Identifies missing values (True/False).
sum()
Counts missing values when combined with isnull().
fillna(value)
Replaces missing values with a specific value.
dropna()
Deletes entire rows containing missing values.

These measures aim to find the center or typical value of a dataset. The three
common measures are Mean, Median, and Mode.

1. Mean (Average)
The arithmetic average. It is calculated by adding all values together and dividing by
the total number of observations. It uses every single data value.

⚠️ The Flaw of the Mean
The mean is heavily distorted by extreme outliers. If 9 people earn $10, and 1
person earns $1,000, the Mean is $109. This makes the group look wealthy,
even though 90% are not! In such cases, Median is better.

The word "deep" is used because data passes through several hidden layers
before the system produces the final output. Each layer learns a different level of
detail from the data.
Early layers: The system may learn simple features (like edges, shapes, colors).
Deeper layers: It combines those simple features to understand more complex
patterns (like a whole face or a specific car model).
Real-World Example: Photo Gallery Search
A modern photo gallery app on a smartphone uses deep learning to recognize faces,
objects, or places in thousands of photos. When a user types "car" or "flower" in the search
bar, the app instantly shows related photos because its deep neural network has already
learned visual patterns from millions of training images.

i) Authentication / Identity Verification
Confirming the identity of a user before allowing access. This is done via
Username/Password, PIN, OTP (One-Time Password), or Biometrics (Fingerprint/Face).
Example: A banking app sending an OTP to your phone before login.
ii) Access Control
Deciding what an authenticated user is allowed to do (View, Edit, Comment, Download,
Share).
Example: A teacher sharing a Google Doc with students as "view only", but giving group
leaders "edit" permissions.
Secure Collaboration (Continued)
iii) Accountability and Tracking
Ensuring user actions are linked to verified accounts. It helps track who opened, edited,
deleted, or shared a file.
Example: A school LMS tracking exactly which teacher uploaded an assignment and which
student submitted it.
iv) Data Privacy
Protecting personal and sensitive information and using it only for the purpose it was
collected. It involves:
Protection: Keeping names, numbers, marks, and passwords secure.
Controlled Sharing: Sharing only with the right people.
Confidentiality: Data remains private during storage and transmission.
Compliance: Following legal and ethical rules for data handling.
v) Safe Communication / Transmission
Exchanging information through digital platforms securely, protecting messages from
unauthorized interception or wiretapping.
Example: A teacher sharing class instructions through an official, encrypted LMS rather than
an open public forum.

5.5.1 Functions of Equity and Equal Access
Providing Need-Based Support (Equity): Giving help tailored to individuals (e.g., audio

Removing Barriers: Helping students in remote areas of Pakistan attend online
classes by providing mobile-friendly, low-data apps.
Enabling Active Participation: Providing recorded lectures so students who face
power or internet outages don't fall behind.
Supporting Different Learning Needs: Offering videos, text notes, and audio so
students can learn in the way that suits them best.

Summary of Chapter 5
Machine Learning: A model that acts as a trained brain, learning from data to give
outputs without explicit programming for every scenario.
Neural Networks: Computer models inspired by the human brain, utilizing Input layers,
Hidden layers, Neurons, Weights, Bias, and Output layers.
Deep Learning: An advanced ML method using multi-layer (deep) neural networks,
requiring massive data and high computing power (GPUs).
AI Applications: Face unlock, Speech recognition, NLP (translation/chatbots),
Healthcare image analysis, Autonomous vehicles, and Fraud detection.
Secure Collaboration: Safely working online by enforcing Authentication (verifying
identity) and Access Control (managing permissions).
Data Privacy & Protection: Protecting sensitive data using Encryption (changing data
to ciphertext), strong passwords, firewalls, and regular backups.
Security Threats: Includes Malware (viruses/Trojans), Phishing (fake emails stealing
info), DoS (crashing servers with fake traffic), and Human Error.
Mitigation: Preventive measures like 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication), Antivirus
software, and strong user awareness training.
Equity vs Equal Access: Equal access gives everyone the same tools. Equity gives
specific, tailored support to those who need it (e.g., captions for the hearing impaired)
to ensure fair participation in digital spaces.

truthfulness, and fairness when collecting user feedback. They should not collect
unnecessary personal information or share phone numbers/photos without permission.

Summary of Chapter 6
Entrepreneurship: The process of identifying a problem and testing/improving a
solution (product/service) until it becomes useful.
Digital Age: Entrepreneurs use accessible digital tools (social media, forms,
websites) to start and test ideas quickly with low investment.
Business Ideas: A good idea comes from observing daily life problems and
talking directly to users.
Prototype: An early model used to show and test the design of an idea. Can be
Low-Fidelity (paper), Mid-Fidelity (PowerPoint), or High-Fidelity (realistic code).
Development Cycle: Consists of Design, Build, Test, and Iterate. Feedback is
crucial for improvement.
MVP (Minimum Viable Product): The simplest working version of a product used
to test real market demand and user behavior.
Prototype vs MVP: Prototype tests "Does it look right?", MVP tests "Will people
actually use it?".
Riskiest Assumption: The core belief that, if wrong, will cause the business to fail.
Must be tested early.
Beachhead Market: A small, focused group of first users with a strong need for
the product. Easier to reach and learn from than a broad market.
Ethics & Equity: Digital solutions must respect user privacy, be truthful, and
consider accessibility for users with limited resources or language barriers.
